Haḷebīḍu
(‘old town’)
------------------------------------------
The finest specimens of Hoysala temple architecture are to be found at Belur and हऌएबीडु (also spelt as Haḷebīḍ), in the Hasan district of Karnataka State.
हऌएबीडु">Temple entrance at HaḷebīḍuKnown earlier as Dvārasamudra, हऌएबीडु was a flourishing capital city of the Hoysala dynasty (12th cent. A. D.). After Malik Kafur, the Muslim general of Alla Ud Din, invaded South India, Dvārasamudra was ransacked and it never regained its old glory. Hence it came to be known as ‘Haḷeya Bīḍu’ or ‘Haḷebīḍu’ (old capital or old town). It is now a deserted village about 16 kms. (10 miles) to the east of the Belur town.
The most important temple complex is that of Hoysaḷeśvara. Its construction must have been started around A.

but was not completed.
It is actually a twin temple built in soap-stone, of Hoysaḷeśvara and Śānta-leśvara, the deities (Śivaliṅgas) being named after the king Viṣṇuvardhana (who was Hoysaḷeśvara or the king of the Hoysaḷa dynasty) and his queen Śāntalā. The two sanctums, each hexagonal in shape, stand on the same platform, side by side. They are connected by a transept. There are separate navaraṅgas (assembly halls). The walls, all round, are covered with hundreds of carved figures depicting the various scenes from the two epics. The pillars are round in shape and highly polished.
The Śivaliṅgas are quite big in size.
The other temples in हऌएबीडु are: the Kedāreśvara temple of three rooms but without any icon; the Vīra-bhadra temple and the रङ्गनाथ (Viṣṇu) temple.
There are three Jain temples also, dedicated to पार्श्वनाथ, Śāntinātha and आदिनाथ.
